question: A health headline and its first lines, worded the way many are. Which words did the research not support?
answer: Most of them. Sumner and colleagues traced 462 university press releases to their papers and the news that followed: about a third of the releases already overstated causes, advice or animal results. When the release exaggerated, the news usually did too; when it was accurate, mostly so was the news.
move: Trace a claim back one step before blaming the last messenger.
ask: When I'm annoyed at how something was reported, have I checked where the spin began?

scene.head: Daily news
scene.title: Coffee linked to longer life
scene.body: Three cups a day could add years to your life, says a breakthrough study. Caffeine was linked to longer lifespans in mice.

phrases.text: could add years to your life
phrases.plain: has not been tested on you
phrases.why: Could is a word that can't be wrong. No person was in this study.
Breakthrough is rarely the paper's word. It tends to arrive in the press release.
Linked means seen together. It doesn't say which causes which, or whether either does.
About a third of press releases stretched animal results or causes; the news followed.

scene.ask: Two words at the end undo the headline. Which?
scene.watch: Read a health story from the end: who was studied, and was it cause or only a link?

reference: Sumner et al., The association between exaggeration in health related science news and academic press releases, BMJ 349:g7015, 2014
